title: DOES GOD REALLY REQUIRE PASTORS, ELDERS, AND DEACONS—OR HAVE WE BEEN DEFENDING CHURCH TRADITIONS THAT SCRIPTURE NEVER COMMANDED?
paragraphs: DOES GOD REALLY REQUIRE PASTORS, ELDERS, AND DEACONS—OR HAVE WE BEEN DEFENDING CHURCH TRADITIONS THAT SCRIPTURE NEVER COMMANDED?

What if the greatest danger facing the Church isn't having the wrong leadership structure… but having the right titles in the hands of people who no longer resemble Jesus? A biblical examination of 1 Timothy 3:1–13 and Titus 1:5–9 that may challenge what you believe about spiritual authority, expose the wounds religious leadership can leave behind, and remind us who truly owns the Church.
There is a kind of pain that only someone wounded inside a church can understand.
It is the pain of walking into a place where you expected to find the love of Jesus, only to discover power struggles, favoritism, manipulation, and spiritual pride.
It is the confusion of watching someone preach humility from a pulpit while demanding unquestioning loyalty behind closed doors.
It is the heartbreak of seeing faithful believers quietly disappear because the people entrusted with caring for their souls became the very people who wounded them.
And sometimes, the deepest wound comes from a question nobody seems willing to answer.
Did God actually command the Church to operate this way?
Must every congregation have a senior pastor, a board of elders, and a separate group of deacons?
Is a church spiritually defective if its leadership looks different?
Can a congregation faithfully follow Jesus without copying the organizational structure of another denomination?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all…
What happens when a church has every biblical title but has forgotten the biblical character those titles were supposed to represent?
Before we answer, we need to settle something that changes everything.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood to establish a religious empire built around human personalities. He gave His life to redeem a people who belong to Him.
The Church is not ultimately the pastor's possession.
It is not the elders' kingdom.
It is not the deacons' organization.
It is not the property of the loudest donor, the founding family, or the most influential committee.
The Church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And when we forget that, even a structure that looks biblical on paper can become spiritually destructive in practice.
Listen carefully to what Paul told the elders of Ephesus in Acts 20:28:
"Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood." (KJV)
Did you notice?
The flock belongs to God.
The overseers are entrusted with its care.
And the price of that flock was not a building fund, a denominational charter, or an impressive ministry résumé.
It was blood.
The blood of Christ.
That means church leadership is not merely an administrative question.
It is a sacred stewardship involving people for whom Jesus died.
And that is precisely why Scripture takes leadership so seriously.
In 1 Timothy 3:1, Paul writes:
The Greek expression translated "office of a bishop" is ἐπισκοπῆς (episkopēs), referring here to the responsibility or office of oversight.
The related word ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos) means an overseer.
Notice what Paul calls this aspiration.
A good work.
Not a prestigious title.
Not a platform for personal ambition.
Not permission to control other people's lives.
A work.
A responsibility.
A calling that demands sacrifice.
The person who desires spiritual oversight should desire the labor of caring for God's people, not merely the recognition that comes with being called a leader.
And that distinction matters more than many of us realize.
Because there are people who want to be called shepherds but have little patience for sheep.
People who want authority without accountability.
People who love the microphone but avoid the hospital room.
People who enjoy being honored publicly but resist correction privately.
And sometimes, tragically, churches mistake charisma for calling.
But Paul does something remarkable.
He does not begin his qualifications for overseers by demanding impressive speaking skills, business experience, financial success, popularity, or a commanding personality.
He begins with character.
"A bishop then must be blameless…" (1 Timothy 3:2, KJV)
The Greek word ἀνεπίλημπτον (anepilēmpton) carries the sense of being above reproach—not sinlessly perfect, but not legitimately open to discrediting accusation through one's conduct.

Paul continues by describing someone who must be sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not violent, not greedy, gentle, not quarrelsome, and capable of managing his household well.
Then comes a warning that should make every ambitious religious leader examine his heart.
"Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil." (1 Timothy 3:6, KJV)
Pride.
Not lack of talent.
Not insufficient influence.
Pride.
The very sin that can turn spiritual responsibility into spiritual self-exaltation.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
Have we sometimes promoted people because they were gifted before we knew whether they were godly?
Have we confused the ability to attract a crowd with the maturity to care for a soul?
Have we celebrated ministries growing larger while failing to ask whether their leaders were growing more like Christ?
A crowded church is not automatically a healthy church.
A gifted preacher is not automatically a qualified overseer.
And a respected religious title does not automatically mean the person holding it is walking faithfully with God.
But this raises another question.
If Scripture describes overseers, elders, and deacons, does that mean every church must have three separate categories of leadership?
This is where careful Bible reading becomes essential.
In Titus 1:5, Paul tells Titus:
"For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee." (KJV)
The Greek word for elders is πρεσβυτέρους (presbyterous), from presbyteros, a term that can refer to an older person or, in this context, a recognized leader within the church.
Paul clearly expects elders to be appointed.
This is not presented as an optional cultural decoration.
He considers their appointment part of putting unfinished matters in order among the churches in Crete.
But watch what happens next.
In Titus 1:7, while explaining the qualifications of these elders, Paul writes:
The Greek here uses ἐπίσκοπον (episkopon)—overseer.
Did you catch that?
Paul begins by speaking about elders.
Then, while describing their qualifications, he calls the leader an overseer.
The natural reading is that the same leadership responsibility is being described from related perspectives.
"Elder" emphasizes the recognized person or position, while "overseer" emphasizes the responsibility of supervision and care.
This connection becomes even clearer in Acts 20.
In verse 17, Paul summons the elders of the church in Ephesus.
In verse 28, he tells those same men that the Holy Spirit has made them overseers and commands them to shepherd God's flock.
Elders.
Overseers.
Shepherding.
Three expressions connected within the same leadership ministry.
And 1 Peter 5:1–3 reinforces this pattern.
Peter addresses the elders and urges them to feed, or shepherd, the flock of God, exercising oversight willingly and not for shameful gain.
He warns them against acting as lords over those entrusted to them.
Then he points them toward the Chief Shepherd.
Jesus Christ.
This is crucial.
The New Testament does not clearly require every congregation to establish three separate ruling offices called pastor, elder, and bishop.
In these passages, elder and overseer refer to closely connected, and apparently overlapping, leadership responsibilities. Shepherding describes a central part of their work.
The Greek word ποιμήν (poimēn) means shepherd or pastor.

In Ephesians 4:11, pastors are mentioned among Christ's gifts to His Church. The verse emphasizes their role in equipping God's people, while Acts 20 and 1 Peter 5 connect shepherding with the work of elders and overseers.

This is why many Christians understand pastors, elders, and overseers as descriptions of the same basic New Testament leadership office, though different traditions distinguish their functions in different ways.
But we must be careful.
The fact that these terms overlap does not mean every historical disagreement about church government disappears.
Christians who hold congregational, presbyterian, and episcopal understandings of church leadership interpret the broader biblical evidence differently.
Some emphasize the congregation's responsibility in recognizing leaders and exercising discipline.
Others emphasize shared oversight by a plurality of elders.
Still others see biblical foundations for broader oversight across multiple congregations.
Those disagreements deserve serious biblical examination, not careless accusations that every Christian who differs from us has abandoned Scripture.
Nevertheless, one truth stands firmly.

The New Testament gives real instructions about church leadership, but it does not provide an exhaustive organizational chart specifying every modern title, committee, reporting relationship, or administrative procedure.
That means churches have some freedom in how they organize their ministries.
But freedom is not permission to ignore what God has revealed.
A church may arrange its administration differently from another faithful congregation.
It may have a full-time preaching pastor, several elders, ministry coordinators, and deacons.
It may be a small congregation that has not yet developed all the leadership capacity it needs.
It may meet in a home rather than a large building.
It may operate within a broader network of congregations.
But none of those differences automatically settles whether it is faithful to Scripture.
The deeper questions remain.
Are spiritually qualified people providing genuine oversight?
Is God's Word being faithfully taught?
Are the vulnerable being protected?
Is the congregation being equipped to follow Jesus?
Are leaders accountable?
And is Christ being honored as the true Head of His Church?
Because a church can reproduce the terminology of the first century while violating the spirit of the instructions given to the first-century Church.
And the opposite danger also exists.
A congregation may claim that leadership structures are merely human inventions and use that claim to dismiss the biblical need for qualified oversight altogether.
That is not faithfulness either.
Paul did not tell Titus to leave the churches of Crete permanently without recognized elders because leadership was unnecessary.
He told him to appoint them.
Acts 14:23 likewise describes Paul and Barnabas appointing elders in the churches.
Philippians 1:1 addresses the saints in Philippi together with overseers and deacons.
And 1 Timothy 3 provides qualifications for both overseers and deacons.
These passages demonstrate that recognized leadership and accountable service were normal, important features of apostolic church life.
The precise organizational arrangements may vary.
The biblical responsibilities cannot simply be discarded.
And this brings us to deacons.
In 1 Timothy 3:8, Paul writes:
The Greek term διάκονος (diakonos) fundamentally means servant or minister, with its precise sense depending on context.
It can describe service broadly, but in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3 it appears to identify recognized servants or ministers within the congregation.
Paul requires them to be dignified, sincere, morally disciplined, faithful, and tested.
He also addresses their households and conduct.
Why would Paul establish such serious qualifications for people serving in the church?
Because service in God's household is never spiritually insignificant.
We sometimes imagine that the most important person in a church is the one standing behind the pulpit.
But consider the quiet believer who brings food to a struggling widow.
The faithful servant who helps distribute assistance without humiliating the poor.
The person who makes sure an elderly member is not forgotten.
The worker who handles church resources with integrity when nobody is watching.
These acts may never produce applause.
But they matter deeply to Christ.
Acts 6:1–6 provides an important example of the apostles arranging for qualified men to address a practical crisis involving the daily distribution to widows.
The passage does not explicitly call these seven men deacons, so we should not pretend it settles every question about the later office.
Yet it clearly demonstrates that practical service, wise delegation, spiritual character, and the protection of neglected people mattered in the earliest Christian community.
And here is something worth remembering.
The Greek word associated with service does not make service inferior.
Jesus Himself declared:
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45, KJV)
The Lord of glory came to serve.
Think about that.
The One before whom every knee will one day bow did not enter this world demanding the privileges of earthly royalty.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed children.
He fed the hungry.
He washed feet.
He bore a cross.
And now we dare to imagine that serving others is beneath someone with a church title?
Something has gone terribly wrong when leadership becomes a ladder toward personal importance rather than a descent into Christlike service.
But perhaps the hardest question is still ahead.
What if your church has a pastor, elders, and deacons—and the leadership is still spiritually unhealthy?
What if the titles are biblical but the behavior is not?
What if people are told to submit to authority while their leaders refuse to submit to Scripture?
What if legitimate questions are treated as rebellion?
What if wounded members are silenced because protecting the institution has become more important than protecting the flock?
The Bible does command believers to respect and respond appropriately to faithful spiritual leadership.
Hebrews 13:17 speaks of leaders who watch over souls as those who must give an account.
But that accountability is precisely why leadership must never be treated as absolute.
Human shepherds are accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
Church authority is real, but it is subordinate to Christ and His Word.
And the Bible does not instruct believers to conceal wrongdoing simply because the person responsible holds a respected religious office.
In 1 Timothy 5:19–20, Paul gives instructions concerning accusations against elders and the public rebuke of those who persist in sin.
The requirement for proper witnesses protects against careless accusations, while the command to address established wrongdoing prevents leaders from being treated as untouchable.
Biblical accountability protects both justice and truth.
It is not a license for gossip.
Neither is it a shield for abuse.
And when someone uses spiritual authority to intimidate, exploit, or harm others, that behavior must not be excused as ordinary pastoral leadership.
Jesus never authorized shepherds to devour His sheep.
Perhaps you have experienced something like this.
You once loved going to church.
You volunteered without being asked.
You gave what you could.
You prayed for your leaders.
You believed you were part of a spiritual family.
Then something happened.
Maybe you asked a sincere question and were made to feel disloyal.
Maybe you witnessed favoritism that nobody wanted to confront.
Maybe you saw a struggling member treated like a problem rather than a person.
Maybe your own suffering became inconvenient to people who preferred a polished religious image.
And eventually, you stopped speaking.
Then you stopped serving.
Then you stopped attending.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether Jesus Himself was as harsh as the people who claimed to represent Him.
If that is part of your story, please hear this.
The failures of a human shepherd do not change the character of the Good Shepherd.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy that wounded you.
He is not the manipulation that exhausted you.
He is not the pride that dismissed your pain.
He is not the religious performance that made you feel invisible.
He is the Savior who knows His sheep.
In John 10:11, Jesus says:
"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." (KJV)
The Greek is profoundly beautiful:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
"I am the good shepherd."
The adjective καλός (kalos) communicates goodness, nobility, or excellence in this context.
Jesus is not merely claiming to be another competent religious leader.
He identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd whose sacrificial care distinguishes Him from those who abandon or exploit the flock.
And the difference is staggering.
False shepherds sacrifice the sheep to preserve themselves.
Jesus sacrificed Himself to save the sheep.
False shepherds use people to build their names.
Jesus gave His life to redeem people for His Father.
False shepherds fear losing control.
Jesus willingly laid down His life and took it up again.
That is the standard against which every Christian leader must be measured.
Not fame.
Not wealth.
Not organizational size.
Not the number of followers on social media.
Not the ability to silence criticism.
Christlikeness.
And we must not miss the Gospel while discussing church government.
Because the deepest problem in the Church is not simply organizational confusion.
It is sin.
The same sin that corrupts politics, families, businesses, and nations can also corrupt religious leadership.
Pride.
Greed.
Deception.
Envy.
Selfish ambition.
The hunger to be admired.
The desire to control.
And those sins are not confined to pastors or elders.
They live in the human heart.
Sometimes even in ours.
We can criticize an arrogant pastor while secretly craving recognition ourselves.
We can condemn controlling leaders while refusing correction in our own lives.
We can demand accountability from others while hiding our own compromises.
That is why the answer cannot simply be a better organizational chart.
The Church needs something far deeper.
We need repentance.
We need the grace of God.
We need the cleansing of Christ.
We need the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
And we need to return again and again to the cross.
Because at Calvary, Jesus did not merely expose human sin.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve so that all who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
The cross declares both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
That is the heart of our message.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because wrongdoing should be hidden.
Not because forgiveness eliminates the need for justice, restitution, or accountability.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners, restore the repentant, heal the wounded, and build His Church through the truth of His Gospel.
Grace does not turn evil into good.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who can transform their lives.
And sometimes that transformation begins with a leader admitting, "I was wrong."
Sometimes it begins with a congregation refusing to excuse what Scripture condemns.
Sometimes it begins with a wounded believer discovering that Jesus has not abandoned them.
And sometimes it begins with an entire church asking a question it should have asked long ago.
Are we organizing ourselves around the teachings of Christ, or around the preservation of human power?
That question deserves an answer.
So does the original question.
Does the Bible require churches to have pastors, elders, and deacons, or can leadership structures vary?

The most faithful answer is that the New Testament establishes recognized, qualified oversight and service as important patterns of church life, while allowing more room for organizational variation than some modern church systems acknowledge.
Paul's instructions in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are not disposable suggestions.
Churches should take seriously the appointment and recognition of biblically qualified leaders.
The New Testament repeatedly presents elders or overseers caring for congregations, and it recognizes deacons as servants with significant qualifications.
The evidence also strongly connects the ministries of elder, overseer, and shepherd, rather than requiring that pastor, elder, and bishop always be three separate offices.
At the same time, Scripture does not prescribe every detail of modern governance.
It does not require a particular corporate board arrangement, a specific job title such as "senior pastor," a universal staff hierarchy, or one denominational administrative system.
There is also a distinction between a congregation temporarily lacking qualified leaders and a congregation permanently rejecting the biblical responsibility for spiritual oversight.
The former may be an unfinished situation requiring prayer, patience, and wise development.
The latter raises a serious question about obedience to the apostolic pattern.

The New Testament often describes elders in the plural, and that evidence deserves careful attention. Yet Christians differ over how plurality should be implemented in every congregation and how leadership responsibilities relate to the wider church.

Even the interpretation of some qualifications remains debated among serious Bible readers. For example, the expression "husband of one wife" in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 is commonly understood as emphasizing marital faithfulness, though churches differ over its precise implications for unmarried, widowed, or remarried candidates.

Similarly, 1 Timothy 3:11 is understood by some as referring to deacons' wives and by others as referring to women serving as deacons. Romans 16:1 describes Phoebe as a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, an important passage in that discussion.
These questions should be examined with humility, attention to the original language, and respect for the full witness of Scripture.
We should not claim certainty where faithful interpreters recognize genuine difficulties.
Nor should we use interpretive disagreements as an excuse to ignore what is clear.
And what is clear?
Church leaders must be spiritually qualified.
They must serve rather than dominate.
They must teach and guard sound doctrine.
They must care for God's people.
They must resist greed, arrogance, and abuse of authority.
They must remember that they will answer to Christ.
And the whole congregation must remember that its ultimate allegiance belongs to Jesus.
Not a denomination.
Not a personality.
Not a ministry brand.
Jesus.
That truth should humble every pastor.
It should sober every elder.
It should dignify every deacon.
It should protect every congregation.
And it should give hope to every believer who has wondered whether the Church can still reflect the beauty of its Savior.
Because the answer is yes.
Not through perfect human leaders.
Not through flawless institutions.
But through the grace of God working in people who continually submit themselves to His Word.
Picture a church where pastors do not need to pretend they are incapable of making mistakes.
Where elders are known for wisdom rather than intimidation.
Where deacons serve without craving applause.
Where members can ask sincere questions without being humiliated.
Where accusations are handled justly.
Where wrongdoing is confronted.
Where repentance is welcomed without abandoning accountability.
Where the weak are not forgotten.
Where the poor are not treated as an inconvenience.
Where the Bible is opened with reverence.
Where the Gospel is proclaimed without compromise.
And where everyone, from the newest believer to the most experienced leader, understands one thing.
We are all standing on the same ground at the foot of the cross.
That is not a fantasy of a perfect church.
It is a picture of the kind of faithfulness toward which Scripture calls us, even while we recognize that every congregation still needs God's sanctifying grace.
And perhaps this article has brought a particular face to your mind.
A pastor who needs encouragement to lead faithfully.
An elder who needs to remember that authority is stewardship.
A deacon who quietly serves and rarely hears the words "thank you."
A believer who has been wounded by church leadership.
A friend who stopped attending because they confused the failures of Christians with the heart of Christ.
Or perhaps the person who needs to hear this most is you.
Bring it before God.
Ask Him whether your understanding of church leadership has been shaped more by Scripture or by what you have always known.
Ask Him to reveal any pride, bitterness, fear, or resentment that needs to be surrendered.
And if you have been hurt, ask Him for the courage to seek healing without pretending that what happened was acceptable.
You do not have to call wrongdoing righteousness in order to believe in the power of forgiveness.
You do not have to abandon biblical accountability in order to extend grace.
And you do not have to stop loving the Church because you have witnessed its failures.
Christ still loves His Church.
He is still sanctifying His people.
He is still calling shepherds to faithfulness.
And He is still worthy of our trust.
Or, if you have been wounded and are still seeking healing, you can simply comment, "Christ is still healing me."
You do not have to share details you are not ready to share. A few honest words may be enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
The Church needs to recognize godly leadership as well as confront its failures.
Someone may be considering abandoning fellowship altogether.
Someone may be preparing to enter church leadership without understanding the weight of that calling.
Someone may have spent years believing that questioning an unhealthy leadership practice is the same as questioning God.
And someone may simply need to be reminded that Jesus is better than the worst example of Christianity they have ever encountered.
Our desire is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to help more people know, love, and faithfully follow Jesus Christ.
We want biblical learning and spiritual encouragement to remain accessible to people who need them, including those who cannot afford to purchase Christian resources.
But maintaining, developing, and expanding ministry resources requires ongoing work and support.
It helps sustain the ministry, supports the continued development of resources, and makes it possible to reach more people with Scripture-centered encouragement.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As Paul writes:
Your worth before God is not measured by a monthly payment.
You are welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But the greatest value of this community will never be merchandise or exclusive recognition.
It is the opportunity to keep growing in the Word of God and help others do the same.
What matters is not that everyone gives in the same way.
What matters is that our hearts remain surrendered to Christ.
Because the Church does not need another generation of believers who know every religious title but have forgotten the Savior those titles are meant to serve.
It needs people who know the Scriptures.
People who love the truth.
People who practice repentance.
People who extend grace without excusing evil.
People who serve when nobody applauds.
People who lead without needing to be worshiped.
People who refuse to make human authority greater than the Word of God.
And people who understand that the future of the Church does not rest upon the brilliance of its leaders.
It rests in the hands of its risen Lord.
Jesus said:
"I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." (Matthew 16:18, KJV)
He did not say that His Church would never experience scandal.
He did not promise that every leader would remain faithful.
He did not suggest that every congregation would always organize itself wisely.
But He declared that He would build His Church.
And His promise remains.
So when you look at a congregation, do not stop at the titles on the office doors.
Look for the fruit of Christlike leadership.
Look for faithfulness to the Word.
Look for humility.
Look for integrity.
Look for genuine love.
Look for servants who understand that the flock is precious because the Shepherd gave His life for it.
And above all, look to Jesus.
The Good Shepherd.
The Chief Shepherd.
The Head of the Church.
The crucified and risen Savior.
Because when human shepherds fail, the Good Shepherd remains faithful.
When institutions disappoint, His Gospel remains true.
When sin is exposed, His grace still calls people to repentance.
And when the Church remembers who truly owns it, there is hope for renewal.
The Church was never meant to be a throne for men who crave power. It was purchased by a King who wore a crown of thorns.
